VII Honeycomb lattice

The ground state of the large-UU Hubbard model on the honeycomb lattice at half-filling has long-range Néel order, as for the square lattice. Also as for the square lattice, adding frustrating interactions leads to a phase with VBS (i.e. Kekulé) order [64, 65, 66]. But in contrast to the square lattice, at smaller UU the honeycomb lattice features a semi-metal phase with no broken symmetry, and an electronic dispersion with 2 massless Dirac fermion points in the Brillouin zone.

In this section we extend the SU(2) gauge theory analysis to the honeycomb lattice. We find just the three phases noted above, with no additional superconducting or charge-ordered phases. This difference from the square lattice case can be traced to the fact that the bosonic chargons, BB, move in a background zero flux on the honeycomb lattice [68]. Consequently, the BB dispersion has only a single minimum in the Brillouin zone, and the Higgs phase where BB is condensed breaks no symmetries and realizes the Dirac semi-metal. We sketched a phase diagram for the honeycomb lattice SU(2) gauge theory in Fig. 2.

The details of such a theory have previously been worked out in Ref. 68, but with the interpretation of the deconfined phase as being stable - our interpretation is that this phase is ultimately unstable to either Néel or VBS order. The low energy theory consists of Nf=2N_{f}=2 Dirac fermions with an emergent SO​(5)\text{SO}(5) symmetry rotating between Néel and Kekulé VBS order. As there is only a single minima of the chargon disperion at 𝒌=(0,0)\bm{k}=(0,0), the spinons are coupled to Nb=1N_{b}=1 bosonic chargons, with the full symmetry of the low-energy action being SO​(5)×SU​(2)\text{SO}(5)\times\text{SU}(2), with the SU​(2)\text{SU}(2) chargon symmetry corresponding to the pseudospin. An important point which is not explicitly discussed in Ref. 68 is the possibility of symmetry-allowed quartic interactions between the chargons and spinons, which would be marginal at tree level. However, this is rather simple to rule out due to the fact that the chargon minima is at 𝒌=(0,0)\bm{k}=(0,0), and hence transforms trivially under all the lattice symmetries (an exception are transformations which exchange the AA and BB sublattice, where the sublattice structure of the chargon eigenvalue causes the chargon to acquire a minus sign - this has no effect on chargon bilinears). As a result, symmetry-allowed chargon/spinon quartic interactions demand that the spinon bilinear component is independently allowed by symmetry, and one can easily verify that no such term exists.

The large-Nf,NbN_{f}\,,N_{b} expansion proceeds identically to the one discussed previously in the paper, with the exception that the chargon sector does not contain any quartic interactions aside from a B4B^{4} term (in other words, we take v=0v=0). The results for the various scaling dimensions in Section VI carry over to this scenario, although some of the chargon bilinears studied can only be defined for even NbN_{b}.

We note an interesting relation between the model of Ref. 76 and the SU(2) gauge field theory with Nf=2N_{f}=2 and Nb=1N_{b}=1. The global symmetry of the quantum field theory of Section III is SO(5)f in the fermionic sector for Nf=2N_{f}=2, and USp(2)/ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} in the bosonic sector for Nb=1N_{b}=1. Ref. 76 considered a honeycomb lattice model in which quantum spin Hall, superconducting, and Dirac semi-metal phases meet at a multicritical point, and proposed a SO(5) Gross-Neveu-Yukawa field theory for the multicriticality. The GNY field theory has no gauge fields, and hence there is an additional SO(3)≅\congUSp(2)/ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} global symmetry which acts on the Dirac fermions. So the global symmetries of our SU(2) gauge field theory at Nf=2N_{f}=2 and Nb=1N_{b}=1 are identical to those of the SO(5) GNY theory. It remains an interesting open question whether these two theories are the same conformal field theory.

VIII Discussion

The discovery of high temperature superconductivity in the cuprates sparked decades of theoretical work on quantum phases proximate to the familiar Néel ordered state of the S=1/2S=1/2 square lattice antiferromagnet. Early work [44] argued that the proximate insulator has valence bond solid (VBS) order. The nature of the Néel-VBS quantum transition has also been extensively studied [77, 78, 46], and recent fuzzy sphere investigations [31] have concluded that it is described by a ‘pseudo-critical’ theory with an approximate conformal symmetry, and a nearly exact global SO(5) symmetry which rotates between the 3+23+2 components of the Néel and VBS orders. One formulation of the pseudo-critical theory has a SU(2) gauge field coupled to Nf=2N_{f}=2 fundamental massless Dirac fermions: we have used the fuzzy sphere results to conclude that this gauge theory confines in the infrared with either Néel or VBS order, and the Néel-VBS transition is weakly first order. The ordering is selected by terms which are formally irrelevant in the continuum theory, and we assume here that Néel order is selected.

The present paper extends these investigations by allowing for charge fluctuations, while remaining at half-filling and preserving particle-hole symmetry. Following earlier work [18], we have shown that adding charge fluctuations to the SU(2) gauge theory leads naturally to a dd-wave superconductor with nodal quasiparticles, and states with period-2 charge order. We can then consider quantum transitions between the Néel state and the dd-wave superconductor, or between the Néel state and charge order. Such transitions are described by a direct extension of the SU(2) gauge theory with Nf=2N_{f}=2 fundamental massless Dirac fermions—there are additional fundamental Nb=2N_{b}=2 massless complex scalars. Given the weakly broken conformal symmetry for Nf=2N_{f}=2, Nb=0N_{b}=0 [73, 32, 31], and the stability of conformal gauge theories at large Nf,bN_{f,b}, it is very plausible that the Nf=2N_{f}=2, Nb=2N_{b}=2 case exhibits true deconfined criticality with an exact emergent conformal symmetry.

The Nf=2N_{f}=2, Nb=2N_{b}=2 quantum field theory studied in this paper is defined by the Lagrangian ℒψ+ℒB\mathcal{L}_{\psi}+\mathcal{L}_{B} in (17) and (21). Here rr is the tuning parameter which takes the system from the Néel state (present when rr is large and positive and BB is not condensed) to the states allowed by charge fluctuations (with dd-wave superconductivity or charge order). The coefficients of the quartic couplings v1,2,3v_{1,2,3} in (21) select among the latter states.

We studied two different large Nf,bN_{f,b} generalizations of this theory, defined by the extensions (23) and (128) in the bosonic sector. The phase diagrams of these theories at Nb=∞N_{b}=\infty appear in Fig. 1. The 1/Nf,b1/N_{f,b} expansions of the second-order quantum phase transitions are described in Section VI and Appendix A. We computed the scaling dimensions of the gauge-invariant order parameters, which are composites of two fermions or two bosons, and the electron operators at momenta (±π/2,±π/2)(\pm\pi/2,\pm\pi/2), which are the composites of one fermion and one boson in (30). Our results are summarized in Table 3. The results are not expected to be accurate at Nf=Nb=2N_{f}=N_{b}=2, when the 1/Nf,b1/N_{f,b} corrections are quite large.

The scaling dimension of the electron operator determines a novel feature of the quantum transition out of the dd-wave superconductor. The dd-wave superconductor itself is conventional, and has 4 nodal points with gapless Bogoliubov quasiparticles. In BCS theory, such gapless quasiparticles are remnants of the Fermi surface of the parent metal, and so the electronic quasiparticle residue remains non-zero across the metal-superconducting transition. However, for the transition from the dd-wave superconductor to the Néel state, there is no longer a simple relationship between the Bogoliubov quasiparticles and the Fermi surface excitations of a parent metal. Instead, the Bogliubov quasiparticles of the superconductor are connected to the spinons of the deconfined quantum critical point. As there are no gapless electronic excitations in the Néel state, and the electronic quasiparticle residue vanishes at the transition out of the dd-waves superconductor with an exponent determined by the scaling dimension of the electron operator at the deconfined quantum critical point.

A recent paper [23] has shown that a similar phenomenon can also happen in the electron doped case in a situation where the normal state has no Fermi surface crossing the zone diagonals: nevertheless, gapless nodal quasiparticles do appear in the proximate dd-wave superconductor, in a region of the Brillouin zone which is gapped in the normal state. Furthermore, there are connections of this remarkable phenomenon to the recent photoemission observations of Ref. 30 on the electron doped cuprates.

Along the same lines, we believe the dd-wave superconductor found in the quasi-one-dimensional numerical study of Ref. 53, by doping the spin liquid of the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} antiferromagnet, will have 4 nodal points in the two-dimensional limit.

Finally, we note the analysis of Section VII, where we applied the same line of thought to the Néel-VBS transition on the honeycomb lattice [64, 65]. We found only a single additional phase upon including charge fluctuations: a Dirac semi-metal with no broken symmetries. All these phases (Néel, VBS (Kekulé), Dirac semi-metal) have been observed in experiments on monolayer graphene [79, 80]. It is interesting to speculate that the absence of a superconducting phase on the honeycomb lattice in our theory, in contrast to the square lattice, is the underlying reason for the low superconducting TcT_{c}’s observed in the graphene family of compounds.

dim​[Ba​s†​Ts​tα​Ba​t]=(1+ηB)+ηvertex=1−163​(2​Nb+Nf)​π2​(NfNb+14).\text{dim}[B^{\dagger}_{as}T^{\alpha}_{st}B_{at}]=(1+\eta_{B})+\eta_{\text{vertex}}=1-\frac{16}{3(2N_{b}+N_{f})\pi^{2}}\left(\frac{N_{f}}{N_{b}}+14\right). (144)

Taking Nf=Nb=2N_{f}=N_{b}=2, the dimension is 1−40/3​π2=−0.351-40/3\pi^{2}=-0.35 which is unfortunately negative but an artifact of the small NN’s chosen. Our anomalous scaling dimension is

ηB2=1−323​(2​Nb+Nf)​π2​(NfNb+14).\eta_{B^{2}}=1-\frac{32}{3(2N_{b}+N_{f})\pi^{2}}\left(\frac{N_{f}}{N_{b}}+14\right). (145)

A.1.3 Superconducting order parameter

The additional diagram is figure 19.

The relevant integral is the same as −Iλ;2-I_{\lambda;2}. Index summation gives minus three as in the gauge field correction, resulting in

ιvertex=42​Nb​π2​(1+3)−8⋅3(2​Nb+Nf)​π2​(1−ζ)=8Nb​π2−24(2​Nb+Nf)​π2​(1−ζ).\begin{split}\iota_{\text{vertex}}&=\frac{4}{2N_{b}\pi^{2}}(1+3)-\frac{8\cdot 3}{(2N_{b}+N_{f})\pi^{2}}(1-\zeta)\\ &=\frac{8}{N_{b}\pi^{2}}-\frac{24}{(2N_{b}+N_{f})\pi^{2}}(1-\zeta).\end{split} (146)

The dimension of this quadratic boson is thus

dim​[Ba​s​εa​b​Js​t​Bb​t]=(1+ηB)+ιvertex=1+43​(2​Nb+Nf)​π2​(5​NfNb−38),\text{dim}\left[B_{as}\varepsilon_{ab}J_{st}B_{bt}\right]=(1+\eta_{B})+\iota_{\text{vertex}}=1+\frac{4}{3(2N_{b}+N_{f})\pi^{2}}\left(5\frac{N_{f}}{N_{b}}-38\right), (147)

Taking Nf=Nb=2N_{f}=N_{b}=2, the dimension is 1−22/3​π2=0.26.1-22/3\pi^{2}=0.26. Anomalous scaling dimension is then

ιB2=1+83​(2​Nb+Nf)​π2​(5​NfNb−38).\iota_{B^{2}}=1+\frac{8}{3(2N_{b}+N_{f})\pi^{2}}\left(5\frac{N_{f}}{N_{b}}-38\right). (148)

A.1.4 Correlation length exponent

In addition to the diagrams presented in figures 11, now we also have figure 20 due to the HjH_{j} field:

Notice that other diagrams such as replacing the dashed λ\lambda line in diagram 11(d) by the dashdotted HzH_{z} line will cancel each other since we need to sum over boson bubbles with different gauge indices. The self energies corresponding to the above two diagrams are

Σ(g)=−Σ(c),Σ(h)=−Σ(e).\Sigma^{(g)}=-\Sigma^{(c)},\quad\Sigma^{(h)}=-\Sigma^{(e)}. (149)

Both relevant integrals have been evaluated before, leading to

Σ(g)+Σ(h)→−3π2​Nb​λg​log⁡λg.\Sigma^{(g)}+\Sigma^{(h)}\rightarrow-\frac{3}{\pi^{2}N_{b}}\lambda_{g}\log\lambda_{g}. (150)

Combining with the v=0v=0 results, we now have the modified total coefficient

α=−3Nb​π2−12π2​(7​Nf−18​Nb(Nf+2​Nb)2+ζNf+2​Nb).\alpha=-\frac{3}{N_{b}\pi^{2}}-\frac{12}{\pi^{2}}\left(\frac{7N_{f}-18N_{b}}{(N_{f}+2N_{b})^{2}}+\frac{\zeta}{N_{f}+2N_{b}}\right). (151)

The correlation function exponent is then (we also need to use the modified anomalous scaling dimension of BB in (142)):

νB≈1+73​Nb​π2−20(2​Nb+Nf)​π2+12π2​7​Nf−18​Nb(2​Nb+Nf)2.\nu_{B}\approx 1+\frac{7}{3N_{b}\pi^{2}}-\frac{20}{(2N_{b}+N_{f})\pi^{2}}+\frac{12}{\pi^{2}}\frac{7N_{f}-18N_{b}}{(2N_{b}+N_{f})^{2}}. (152)

At Nb=Nf=2,N_{b}=N_{f}=2, this is νB=0.037.\nu_{B}=0.037.

A.1.5 Boson-fermion Composite

In the expression dim​[B†​ψ]=dim​[B]+dim​[ψ]+ηB†​ψ=32+ηB+ηψ2+ηB†​ψ,\text{dim}[B^{\dagger}\psi]=\text{dim}[B]+\text{dim}[\psi]+\eta_{B^{\dagger}\psi}=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{\eta_{B}+\eta_{\psi}}{2}+\eta_{B^{\dagger}\psi}, the only change compared with (103) lies in dim[B][B]. The result is thus

dim​[B†​ψ]=32−23​(2​Nb+Nf)​π2​(NfNb+62).\text{dim}[B^{\dagger}\psi]=\frac{3}{2}-\frac{2}{3(2N_{b}+N_{f})\pi^{2}}\left(\frac{N_{f}}{N_{b}}+62\right). (153)

Again other gauge-invariant choices such as ∑a,bBa​s​εa​b​ψb​t\sum_{a,b}B_{as}\varepsilon_{ab}\psi_{bt}, or with γ\gamma matrices inserted give the same result. At Nb=Nf=2N_{b}=N_{f}=2, we have dim[B†​ψ]=32−7π2=0.79.[B^{\dagger}\psi]=\frac{3}{2}-\frac{7}{\pi^{2}}=0.79.

Appendix B Useful integrals

Below we present some details of the integrals that appear in the main text.

We first present more details for the derivation of the effective action in section VI.1. Expansion of the matrix log gives, in the bosonic sector,

Tr​ln⁡𝒢b−1​GB=2Nb∫d3​p(2​π)3d3​q(2​π)3{G(q)δp​0∫d3​p′(2​π)3Aα​μ(p′)Aαμ(−p′)−12G(q)G(q−p)[−λ(p)λ(−p)+∑j(2q−p)μAαμ(p)(2q−p)νAαν(−p)]}.\begin{split}\text{Tr}\ln\mathcal{G}^{-1}_{b}G_{B}=&2N_{b}\int\frac{d^{3}p}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\Bigg\{G(q)\delta_{p0}\int\frac{d^{3}p^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}A_{\alpha\mu}(p^{\prime})A_{\alpha}^{\mu}(-p^{\prime})\\ &\quad\quad-\frac{1}{2}G(q)G(q-p)\bigg[-\lambda(p)\lambda(-p)+\sum_{j}(2q-p)_{\mu}A_{\alpha}^{\mu}(p)(2q-p)_{\nu}A_{\alpha}^{\nu}(-p)\bigg]\Bigg\}.\\ \end{split} (154)

For the fermion sector we have

Trln𝒢f−1Gψ=−Nf2∫d3​p(2​π)3d3​q(2​π)3Tr[Gψ(q)γμAμα(p)σαGψ(p+q)γνAνβ(−p)σβ].\text{Tr}\ln\mathcal{G}^{-1}_{f}G_{\psi}=-\frac{N_{f}}{2}\int\frac{d^{3}p}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\text{Tr}[G_{\psi}(q)\gamma^{\mu}A^{\alpha}_{\mu}(p)\sigma_{\alpha}G_{\psi}(p+q)\gamma^{\nu}A^{\beta}_{\nu}(-p)\sigma_{\beta}]. (155)

The integrals can be evaluated, we summarize the results here:

∫d3​q(2​π)31q2+λ¯=−λ¯4​π,∫d3​q(2​π)3Tr​[γμ​q̸​γν​(p̸+q̸)]q2​(p+q)2=−116​q,∫d3​q(2​π)3​1(q2+λ¯)​((q−p)2+λ¯)=14​π​p​arctan⁡p2​λ¯,∫d3​q(2​π)3​(2​q−p)μ​(2​q−p)ν(q2+λ¯)​((q−p)2+λ¯)=−(δμ​ν+pμ​pνp2)​λ¯4​π−(δμ​ν−pμ​pνp2)​(4​λ¯+p28​p​π​arctan⁡p2​λ¯).\begin{split}&\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{1}{q^{2}+\bar{\lambda}}=-\frac{\sqrt{\bar{\lambda}}}{4\pi},\quad\quad\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{\text{Tr}[\gamma^{\mu}\not{q}\gamma^{\nu}(\not{p}+\not{q})]}{q^{2}(p+q)^{2}}=-\frac{1}{16q},\\ &\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{1}{(q^{2}+\bar{\lambda})\big((q-p)^{2}+\bar{\lambda}\big)}=\frac{1}{4\pi p}\arctan\frac{p}{2\sqrt{\bar{\lambda}}},\\ &\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{(2q-p)_{\mu}(2q-p)_{\nu}}{(q^{2}+\bar{\lambda})\big((q-p)^{2}+\bar{\lambda}\big)}=-\left(\delta_{\mu\nu}+\frac{p_{\mu}p_{\nu}}{p^{2}}\right)\frac{\sqrt{\bar{\lambda}}}{4\pi}-\bigg(\delta_{\mu\nu}-\frac{p_{\mu}p_{\nu}}{p^{2}}\bigg)\bigg(\frac{4\bar{\lambda}+p^{2}}{8p\pi}\arctan\frac{p}{2\sqrt{\bar{\lambda}}}\bigg).\end{split} (156)

The leading correction to the free energy is thus (61). Notice the first and second order bosonic contributions to ΠA\Pi_{A} combine to give a simple expression.
